analysis.one_liner: Bars police agencies from buying guns from dealers whose guns repeatedly turn up at crimes.
analysis.headline: Backed by 29 House members, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on September 18, 2025, and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets gun dealers whose firearms repeatedly show up at crimes soon after their last retail sale. It requires the ATF to publish an annual list of dealers with 25 or more of these 'short time-to-crime' traces in at least two of the previous three years, and to alert local police when a gun the agency sold or transferred is later traced to a crime. Any state, territory, or local government receiving federal justice-assistance grants would be barred from buying guns from, or selling guns to, a dealer on that list, and the bill strips old appropriations riders that currently block the ATF from releasing firearms tracing data.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities affected by gun violence gain a transparency tool: they can see which dealers are the source of crime guns, and police agencies are steered away from buying from them. Local police departments also gain direct notice when weapons they disposed of are recovered at crime scenes, helping them spot leaks from their own armories.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public annual list of federally licensed dealers whose firearms have 25 or more traces with a 'short time-to-crime' — three years or less between last retail sale and recovery at a crime scene — in at least two of the previous three years.

Prohibits states, territories, and local governments that receive Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds from transferring firearms to or purchasing firearms from a listed dealer, tying federal grant eligibility to the ban.
Requires the ATF to notify state and local law enforcement agencies when a firearm the agency transferred is used or suspected of being used in a crime, as traced by the National Tracing Center.
Repeals a series of appropriations riders dating back to 2003 that limit the ATF's ability to disclose firearms tracing data to the public.
Removes limits on the ATF's authority to disclose firearms tracing data, opening gun-trace information to public scrutiny.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers with high trace counts lose government business, since police agencies receiving federal grant funds could no longer buy from or sell to them. The firearms trade more broadly loses the current shield that keeps ATF trace data out of public view.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun dealers with many crime-gun traces

drawbacks.text: A dealer lands on the list based on trace counts alone, not any finding of wrongdoing — a gun can be stolen or bought through a straw purchaser and still trace back to the originating dealer.
The purchasing ban only reaches governments receiving Byrne grant funds, so its practical effect depends on how many police agencies buy from the listed dealers.
Police agencies could face a narrower pool of licensed sellers for legitimate firearm purchases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a targeted transparency measure, not a broad gun control bill. It regulates only high-trace dealers' access to one stream of government purchasing and lifts secrecy around federal trace data. The main honest objection is that trace counts are an imperfect proxy for a dealer's own conduct, so some listed dealers may be penalized for crimes they did not cause. The bill's scope is narrow, so both the benefit and the cost are modest compared with comprehensive firearms legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Gabe Amo introduced the bill on September 18, 2025, joined on introduction by 17 other House members.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
It has gathered 28 Democratic cosponsors and no action beyond referral, and the Congress is still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, the status quo persists: dealers and the firearms trade keep the existing limits on public trace data, and police agencies keep current purchasing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms trade keeps the status quo

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 18, 2025, and has taken no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 recorded supporters, including all 28 cosponsors, are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: Dealers with 25 or more short time-to-crime traces in at least two of three years would be publicly named and barred from government firearm sales, costing them police procurement business. The trade's interest in avoiding trace-based scrutiny runs against the public's interest in knowing where crime guns come from.

industries.industry: Firearms industry and gun trade associations
industries.note: The bill repeals appropriations riders that have kept ATF tracing data from public disclosure since 2003, exposing the supply chain for crime guns to public view. Industry groups have historically opposed expanding trace-data disclosure.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no Republican support and no scheduled action. Most bills at this stage die in committee, and that is the likely path unless the committee schedules a hearing or markup.
